fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the specified AlCrFeNiSi powder with an unspecified as-cast base alloy, even though Al and Cr are already constituents of the target composition.
It proposes compositional alloying rather than atmosphere-controlled debinding of DLP-printed powder–resin green bodies.
It addresses oxidation resistance during air exposure rather than residual stress, cracking, porosity, densification, and mechanical performance in additive manufacturing.
The proposed protective oxide mechanism conflicts with the target mechanism, in which particle-surface oxides impede interparticle diffusion and delay consolidation.
The baseline is neither an oxygen-rich-debound DLP specimen nor a conventional high-thermal-load additively manufactured component.
No supporting prior evidence is identified.
The falsification experiment is underspecified and lacks defined measurements, geometry, replication, and quantitative rejection criteria.
explanation: The response is largely unrelated to the target intervention and manufacturing route. Its only limited condition overlap is air exposure near 1000 °C. It omits DLP slurry printing, debinding atmosphere control, the 800–1100 °C/24 h sintering window, miniature layered geometry, carbon and oxygen retention, crack and pore evolution, and compression testing. The predicted oxidation-mass-gain outcome does not address the target finding of crack suppression and comparable compressive strength at a 50 °C lower sintering temperature. Although selective formation of alumina or chromia is a generally plausible oxidation hypothesis, it is unsupported here and does not answer the stated materials-processing problem.
